figures.caption: Figure 1. Safe code rate (%) on Python for 7 commercial LLMs under 3 conditions. Plain: the model receives only the coding question with no security instruction. Baseline: an explicit directive to generate secure code is added to the prompt. Ours: Component I appends a structured CWE activation cue retrieved from the NIST vulnerability catalog. All models are accessed via public APIs in a black-box manner.

Figure 3. Motivating code example: C++ unbounded string copy (CWE120). Given a task that asks to copy a 20-byte string into a 10-byte buffer using strcpy, the baseline model follows the prompt literally (highlighted in red), writing 21 bytes into a 10-byte buffer and corrupting adjacent stack memory. SPARK replaces strcpy with strncpy bounded by sizeof(buffer)-1 and appends an explicit null terminator (highlighted in green), preventing the overflow while preserving the copy semantics required by the task.

Figure 6. Kernel density estimates of the safe margin δ = lsafe − lunsafe for ground-truth (GT) safe code (blue dashed), ground-truth unsafe code (red dashed), and SPARK-generated code (green solid), evaluated on 4 models (columns) and 3 languages (rows). The vertical dotted line marks δ = 0 (judge decision boundary). A generated distribution whose mode lies to the right of this boundary and whose mass overlaps substantially with the ground-truth safe curve indicates that SPARK shifts the model’s output toward the safe half-space.

Figure 7. Effect of CWE retrieval depth on safe code generation (CodeLlama-7B-Instruct). Safe Code Rate (top) and wall-clock inference time (bottom) as a function of the number of CWE entries injected into the prompt (K), evaluated across C++ and Java. Safe Code Rate is measured by the trained judge classifier on the held-out evaluation split. Wall-clock time covers both generation and classification.

Figure 8. t-SNE projection of judge-model hidden states for ground-truth safe code (blue triangles), ground-truth unsafe code (red triangles), and SPARKgenerated code (green circles), evaluated on 4 models (columns) and 3 programming languages (rows). Spatial proximity indicates representational similarity as encoded by the judge classifier. A generated cluster that overlaps with the ground-truth safe region indicates that SPARK successfully steers the model’s output into the security-aligned portion of the judge’s feature space.

TABLE 8. TIME COST OF SPARK, ALL IN SECONDS. Generation COLUMNS GIVE THE WALL-CLOCK TIME FOR EVALUATION ON THE TEST SET UNDER COMPONENT I ALONE VERSUS THE FULL SPARK HARNESS (COMPONENT I + II): ADDING THE DECODING-LEVEL COMPONENT II LEAVES THE TIME ESSENTIALLY UNCHANGED, SO THE PER-TOKEN LOGIT BIAS INCURS NO MEASURABLE OVERHEAD. Precompute IS THE ONE-TIME OFFLINE COST OF BUILDING THE COMPONENT II SAFE DIRECTION ON THE TRAINING SET, WHICH IS REUSED FOR ALL INFERENCE.
